findings.claim: BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up the email case-sensitively (BlockedEmail.where(email: email)) with no normalization, so a blocked address can be bypassed by changing letter case (e.g. Bad@spammers.org vs bad@spammers.org). This is also inconsistent with the case-insensitive domain whitelist/blacklist regex.

verifier.reason: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` on a plain `t.string :email` column (db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:4), an exact case-sensitive match in PostgreSQL, and the value arrives un-normalized from `user.email = params[:email]` (app/models/user.rb:87) via lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13. The domain whitelist/blacklist regex in the same validator is case-insensitive (`Regexp.new(..., true)`, lib/validators/email_validator.rb:20), so the inconsistency is real too.

findings.claim: BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count/last_match_at inside email validation, and users#create runs validations twice (user.valid? then user.save), so one signup attempt is counted twice and causes extra writes.

verifier.reason: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at` and saves on every call (app/models/blocked_email.rb:11-19), and it is called from `EmailValidator#validate_each` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13), which runs on User's email validation (app/models/user.rb:47). `users#create` calls `user.valid?` (app/controllers/users_controller.rb:168) and then `user.save` (:172), each re-running validations with errors cleared, so one signup with a blocked email is counted twice and writes twice.

findings.claim: should_block? is a predicate/validation-time method with write side effects: it increments match_count, sets last_match_at and saves the record on every call.

verifier.reason: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` at app/models/blocked_email.rb:11-19 increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at` and calls `record.save` whenever a matching row exists (not literally every call), and it is invoked during validation from lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 via `validates :email, email: true` in app/models/user.rb. Any `valid?` call or repeated validation on a changed email therefore writes to the database and inflates the stats; the spec shows the counting is intentional.

findings.claim: Blocked-attempt stats written during validation are rolled back when save/save! fails validation inside its transaction, so blocked attempts via User.create_for_email and EmailToken.confirm are never recorded.

verifier.reason: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` updates `match_count`/`last_match_at` with `record.save` (app/models/blocked_email.rb:14-16) from inside User validation (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13), and on Rails 3.2.12 validation runs inside the `save!` transaction, so the `RecordInvalid` raised by `user.save!` at app/models/user.rb:103 and app/models/email_token.rb:53 rolls that update back. This rests on Rails 3.2 transaction semantics read from memory, not a run; the normal signup path still records one match because `user.valid?` runs outside a transaction at app/controllers/users_controller.rb:168.

findings.claim: The match_count update uses a non-atomic read-modify-write (match_count += 1; save), so concurrent attempts lose increments.

verifier.reason: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12-16 loads the record, does `record.match_count += 1` in Ruby and calls `record.save` with no lock, optimistic locking column or SQL-side increment, so two concurrent `should_block?` calls for the same email can both write the same value and lose an increment.

findings.claim: The return value of save in the counter update is ignored.

verifier.reason: app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 calls `record.save` (non-bang) inside `should_block?` and discards the result, so a failed update of `match_count`/`last_match_at` goes unnoticed; the block decision at line 18 does not depend on it, so only the statistics are affected.

findings.claim: The regex @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? lacks boundary/end anchoring, so addresses with domains that extend a whitelisted domain (e.g. user@example.com.evil.com) match the whitelist.

verifier.reason: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:19-21 builds `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` with no `\z` or boundary anchor, so `user@example.com.evil.com` matches a whitelisted `example.com` and passes the check at line 5. The method was moved verbatim from app/models/user.rb by this patch, so the flaw is carried over rather than new.
